speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Good day, everyone, and welcome to this Apple Incorporated Second Quarter Fiscal Year 2012 Earnings Release Conference Call. Today's call is being recorded. At this time, for opening remarks and introductions, I would like to turn the call over to Nancy Paxton, Senior Director of Investor Relations. Please go ahead, ma'am.

speaker: Nancy Paxton
title: Senior Director of Investor Relations
content: Thank you. Good afternoon, and thanks to everyone for joining us. Speaking today is Apple CFO, Peter Oppenheimer; and he'll be joined by Apple CEO, Tim Cook; and Treasurer, Gary Wipfler for the Q&A session with analysts. Please note that some of the information you'll hear during our discussion today will consist of forward-looking statements, including, without limitation, those regarding revenue, gross margin, operating expenses, other income and expense, stock-based compensation expense, taxes, earnings per share and future products. Actual results or trends could differ materially from our forecast. For more information, please refer to the risk factors discussed in Apple's Form 10-K for 2011, the Form 10-Q for the first quarter of fiscal 2012 and the Form 8-K filed with the SEC today along with the attached press release. Apple assumes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements or information, which speak as of their respective dates. I'd now like to turn the call over to Peter Oppenheimer for introductory remarks.

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Thank you, Nancy. We're very pleased to report the results of our outstanding second fiscal quarter. We established new March quarter records for iPhone, iPad and Mac sales, leading to our highest March quarter revenue and earnings ever. Revenue for the quarter was $39.2 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 59%. That's a new record for a March quarter and is second only to the all-time record revenue we reported in the most recent December quarter. The year-over-year increase in March quarter revenue was fueled primarily by very strong growth in iPhone and iPad sales. Operating margin was $15.4 billion, representing 39.3% of revenue. Net income was $11.6 billion, increasing 94% over the prior March quarter's result. The quarter's net income translated to earnings per share of $12.30. Turning to the details of the quarter, I'd like to begin with our Mac products and services. We established new March quarter records for both desktops and portables, combining for a total of 4 million Macs sold. This represents growth of 7% year-over-year compared to IDC's latest published forecast of 2% growth for the global personal computer market in the March quarter. We began and ended the quarter with between 3 and 4 weeks of Mac channel inventory, which is below our target range of 4 to 5 weeks. In February, we released the developer preview of Mountain Lion, the ninth major release of Mac OS X. Mountain Lion will bring popular apps and features from iPad to the Mac, including Messages, Notes, Reminders, Game Center, Notification Center, Share Sheets, Twitter integration and AirPlay Mirroring. We expect Mountain Lion to be available from the Mac App Store in late summer this year. Moving to our music products. We sold 7.7 million iPods compared to 9 million in the year ago quarter. Total iPod sales were ahead of our expectations, and iPod touch continued to account for over half of all iPods sold. iPod's share of the U.S. market for MP3 players remains at over 70% based on the latest monthly data published by MPD, and iPod continued to be the top-selling MP3 player in most countries we track based on the latest data published by GFK. We ended the quarter within our target range of 4 to 6 weeks of iPod channel inventory. The iTunes Store generated all-time record results with revenue of almost $1.9 billion in the March quarter, an increase of 35% year-over-year, thanks to continued strong sales of music, video and apps. We now have a catalog of over 28 million songs and 45,000 movies. I'd now like to turn to iPhone. We were thrilled to sell 35.1 million iPhones compared to 18.6 million in the previous March quarter. That represents 88% year-over-year growth compared to 42% growth for the smartphone market overall in the March quarter based on the latest published estimate from IDC. We experienced very strong iPhone sales growth in all of our segments, led by our Asia Pacific and Japan segments where sales more than doubled year-over-year. We continue to see tremendous momentum in Greater China, where iPhone sales were 5 times the level of the year ago quarter, aided by the launch of the iPhone 4S in China in January and the addition of China Telecom as an iPhone carrier in March. The iPhone 4S is now available in over 100 countries and is sold through over 230 carriers. We ended the quarter with about 8.6 million iPhones in channel inventory, a sequential increase of about 2.6 million units, which placed us within our target range of 4 to 6 weeks of iPhone channel inventory. Recognized revenue from iPhone handset and accessory sales was $22.7 billion during the quarter compared to $12.3 billion in the year ago quarter, an increase of 85%. iPhone momentum in the enterprise has evolved beyond email, calendar and contacts. IT and business line managers across industries see the opportunity to leverage both company and employee-owned devices to improve productivity and efficiencies through iOS in-house app development. In fact, the majority of the Fortune 500 companies who have approved iPhone on their networks are members of the iOS Developer Enterprise Program and are actively deploying in-house applications to their employee base. Turning to iPad. We were very pleased with sales of 11.8 million iPads during the March quarter compared to 4.7 million in the year ago quarter, an increase of 151%. Customers are loving the new iPad with its stunning Retina display, A5X chip with Quad-core graphics and the 5-megapixel iSight camera. The new iPad is now available in over 40 countries, and we saw very strong growth in iPad sales around the world with sales more than doubling in each of our segments. Recognized revenue from sales of iPad and iPad accessories during the quarter was $6.6 billion compared to $2.8 billion in the year ago quarter, an increase of 132%. We ended the quarter with about 2 million iPads in channel inventory, a sequential decrease of about 300,000 units, which placed us below our target range of 4 to 6 weeks of iPad channel inventory. The education market's interest in iPad continues to grow. In the March quarter, we sold more than 2 iPads for every Mac to our U.S. K-12 customers while also generating a record quarter for Mac sales. The San Diego School District purchased 10,000 iPads in the March quarter and plans to purchase over 15,000 more in the June quarter for middle school and high school programs. iPad continues to open doors to new customers with whom Apple previously had no relationship. As we enter the K-12 institution buying season, we're hopeful that iPad will be a popular choice. iPad's momentum in business and government also continues to build. The United States Air Force Air Mobility Command is deploying thousands of iPads to serve as electronic flight bags, storing technical publications and operations information for flight crew members and trainers. Companies such as Bechtel and Balfour Beatty are using iPads in the field for project management and viewing blueprints. And thousands of iPads are being deployed as mobile sales tools by companies such as Roche, Amgen, Bayer and Daiichi Sankyo. Combining iPhone, iPad and iPod touch, we surpassed 365 cumulative iOS device sales, selling more than 50 million in the March quarter. The iOS ecosystem continues to expand and thrive with stores in more than 120 countries. The App Store now offers more than 600,000 apps, including over 200,000 apps specifically for iPad. We were very excited to announce the download of the 25th billionth app in March less than 4 years after the launch of the App Store. And iCloud is off to an incredible start, currently with more than 125 million customers signed up since its launch in October. I'd now like to turn to the Apple retail stores, which also generated record March quarter results. Revenue was $4.4 billion, an increase of 38% over the year ago quarter and was second only to the record quarterly revenue generated in the December quarter. The stores experienced very strong year-over-year growth in iPad and iPhone sales, and they sold 826,000 Macs compared to 797,000 in the year ago quarter. And about half the Macs sold in our stores during the March quarter were to customers who had never owned a Mac before. We opened 2 new stores in the quarter, including our first Netherlands store in Amsterdam and a beautiful new store in Houston. We exited the quarter with 363 stores, nearly one-third of which are outside the United States. With an average of 361 stores open, average revenue per store was $12.2 million compared to $9.9 million in the year ago quarter, an increase of 23%. Segment margin reached a new March quarter record of over $1.1 billion, which was 26.1% of retail revenue. We welcomed 85 million visitors to our stores during the quarter compared to 71 million visitors in the year ago quarter, an increase of 19%. That translates to an average of 18,000 visitors per store per week. Total company gross margin was 47.4%, which was 540 basis points higher than our guidance. About half this difference was driven by lower-than-expected commodity and other costs; about one-quarter was due to stronger-than-expected revenue and product mix, including 35 million iPhones; and the remainder was due to some one-time items that we don't expect to recur in the June quarter. Operating expenses were $3.2 billion and included $361 million in stock-based compensation expense. OI&E was $148 million. Turning to cash. Our cash for short-term and long-term marketable securities totaled $110.2 billion at the end of the March quarter compared to $97.6 billion at the end of the December quarter, a sequential increase of $12.6 billion. And about $74 billion of the cash was offshore at the end of the March quarter. Cash flow from operations was $14 billion. As we indicated last month, subject to board declaration, we expect to announce a dividend of $2.65 per share when we report our third quarter results in July. And we will provide information on the record and payment dates at that time. As we move ahead into the June quarter, I'd like to review our outlook, which includes the types of forward-looking information that Nancy referred to at the beginning of the call. We expect revenue to be about $34 billion compared to $28.6 billion in the June quarter last year. We expect gross margin to be about 41.5%, reflecting approximately $70 million related to stock-based compensation expense. We expect OpEx to be about $3.3 billion, including about $385 million related to stock-based compensation. We expect OI&E to be about $175 million. And we expect the tax rate to be about 25.25%. We are targeting EPS of about $8.68. In closing, we're extremely pleased with our record March quarter performance with earnings nearly doubling year-over-year. The new iPad is off to a tremendous start and is our fastest iPad rollout ever. We're thrilled with the global success of the iPhone 4S, which is now available in more than 100 countries, including China. We remain very confident in our strategy, and we're very excited about the fabulous new products in our pipeline. With that, I'd like to open the call to questions.

speaker: Nancy Paxton
title: Senior Director of Investor Relations
content: Thank you, Peter. Operator, may we have the first question?

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: And your first question will come from Katy Huberty with Morgan Stanley.

speaker: Katy Huberty
title: Analyst, Morgan Stanley
content: As it relates to the June quarter revenue guidance, it implies a sequential downtick that is worse than the guidance message you provided over the last 3 years. So can you just talk about some of the headwinds sequentially you see on the top line in the June quarter relative to March?

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Sure, Katy. It's Peter. The manufacturing processes for the iPhone 4S and the new iPad were very successful for us, resulting in the highest launch supply and the fastest country rollouts we've ever seen for these products. Consequently, we were able to meet demand in the March quarter instead of the June quarter this year, which led to revenue exceeding $39 billion. Unlike last year, we anticipate a sequential decline in revenue this year. I'd like to emphasize five main factors influencing our situation: First, changes in iPhone channel inventory. We increased our iPhone channel inventory by approximately 2.6 million units in the March quarter this year and finished within our target inventory range of about 4 to 6 weeks. Last year, we kept adding new countries in the June quarter, increasing our iPhone channel inventory by an additional 700,000 units during that period. Thus, the combination of these inventory builds from this March and last June will affect the year-over-year comparisons. The second factor is the excellent execution of the iPhone 4S. As mentioned in January, we ended December with a considerable backlog for the iPhone 4S, leading to strong sales in January. We also launched in China and 20 other countries in January, completing the rollout of the iPhone 4S to all current shipping markets, which allowed us to maintain a supply and demand balance by the end of the quarter. The third factor is the impressive execution of our new iPad. We had an outstanding launch with ample supply, selling 3 million units in the first few days and achieving the fastest country rollout ever. This enabled us to meet much more demand for the new iPad in the March quarter compared to last year's iPad 2 launch in the same period, resulting in a shift of iPad sales into March this year compared to last, thus affecting the sequential comparisons. Fourth, we lowered the entry price of the basic iPad to $399. Lastly, we've noticed that the U.S. dollar has strengthened recently, which we expect will impact our sequential comparisons, particularly when compared to last year, when the dollar weakened against most currencies during the same time frame. We just reported the most remarkable March quarter Apple has ever seen, and we feel very optimistic about our business and our product pipeline.

speaker: Katy Huberty
title: Analyst, Morgan Stanley
content: Just as a quick follow-up to number 4, the decrease in iPad price. You already saw a 7% sequential decline in March, which suggests that the uptake of the lower-priced iPad 2 was pretty phenomenal in March. Is that the right way to read it? And what does that demand tell you about the potential to move to lower price points on the iPad over time and see significant incremental demand?

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Look, Katy, we're just learning about the elasticity of demand and the $399 price point. It's doing well. But I have to tell you, the new iPad is on fire, and we're selling them as fast as we can make them. So we'll learn more over this quarter especially as we get through the education buying season, which looks terrific for us especially on the iPad.

speaker: Richard Gardner
title: Analyst, Citigroup
content: I acknowledge that you have once again outperformed the market in Macs. However, I would like to hear your perspective on the slowdown in the year-over-year growth rate within that category and the factors you think may have contributed to it. Is this related to product transitions? Were inventories down from the previous quarter? Is there any impact from iPad cannibalization? Any additional insights you could share would be appreciated.

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Yes, Rich, it's Tim. As you mentioned, we did outgrow the market. Macs grew around 7% while the market rose about 2%. This marks our 24th consecutive quarter of outpacing the market, and we're very pleased with that. The comparison to last year is significantly impacted by the fact that we revamped most of our portable line, including the MacBook Pros, in February 2011, making it a challenging comparison. Last year, portables increased by 53% year-on-year, which makes this comparison particularly difficult. When looking at it sequentially, we also need to consider that we had 14 weeks in the December quarter. Therefore, the 26% year-over-year growth in that quarter is probably closer to 17% when accounting for that extra week. While there was some cannibalization from the iPad and the market is slow, the primary reason for the difference compared to a year ago is this challenging comparison.

speaker: A.M. Sacconaghi
title: Analyst, Sanford Bernstein
content: Could you provide more insight into what you are learning about lower price points for both the iPhone and iPad? I know this was previously addressed, but was the decrease in iPad prices solely related to market mix, or does it also involve expanding your channels to indirect partners? Additionally, Tim, could you discuss customer preferences regarding lower-priced offerings for both the iPhone and iPad? I have a follow-up question as well.

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Sure. Tony, regarding the iPad 2, we are excited about the results we've seen since the price adjustment to $399. However, as Peter mentioned, it's been only a few weeks, so it's too early to draw definitive conclusions. Nevertheless, we believe this price change has opened up demand in the education sector, particularly among price-sensitive customers. We've also noticed a significant increase in demand in several other countries at this price point. Early indications are positive, but I should note that the new iPad faced supply constraints for about three weeks last quarter and continues to be constrained. As a result, we are still assessing the sales mix between the new iPad and the iPad 2. However, the strong early sales of the iPad 2 are encouraging. Regarding the iPhone, we remain pleased with the pricing adjustments made a few months ago for the iPhone 3GS and iPhone 4, which contributed to achieving 35 million in sales, marking our second-highest quarter ever.

speaker: A.M. Sacconaghi
title: Analyst, Sanford Bernstein
content: As a second question, could you share your thoughts on the future of the tablet and PC markets? You've mentioned that you believe tablets will eventually surpass PCs in terms of volume and that these markets are somewhat distinct. There appears to be considerable effort, especially with PC platforms, to merge the PC and tablet experiences, partly due to Windows 8 being a touch-based operating system. Can you explain why you think the PC or Ultrabook markets, along with your MacBook Air and tablet markets, won't converge? Is it unrealistic to envision a device in a couple of years that weighs under 2 pounds, has excellent battery life, and can be used as either a notebook or a tablet in a versatile manner? What are your reasons for believing this product may not materialize or for maintaining that these markets should remain separate?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: I believe that anything can be made to work together, but the challenge is that products involve trade-offs. If you push those trade-offs too far, you can end up with something that disappoints everyone. For example, while you could combine a toaster and a refrigerator, the result likely wouldn't satisfy the user. Our stance is that the tablet market has enormous potential, and we recognized this from the very beginning. We didn’t wait for extensive results; we saw its possibilities in action. The iPad has gained significant traction not only among consumers but also in education and business sectors. It's become widely used, and the applications available are both meaningful and abundant. As the ecosystem improves and we continue to focus on creating excellent products, I believe the potential for growth is vast. Since launching the initial iPad two years ago, we have sold 67 million units, which is notable compared to the time it took us to reach similar sales figures for Macs, iPods, and iPhones. The iPad is a remarkable product with its broad appeal, and I am extremely pleased with our innovation in both the product and its ecosystem. Regarding market forecasts, IDC, Gartner, and Forrester have provided projections, with estimates around 375 million tablets by 2015, roughly matching the current size of the PC market. This indicates that even external analysts are starting to see similar trends. I am confident these predictions will hold true. While I believe there’s still a strong market for the MacBook Air, which we continue to develop, it's aimed at a slightly different audience. Merging these markets could lead to compromises that would fail to satisfy either user group. Some individuals may choose to own both types of devices, which is perfectly fine. However, we aren't pursuing convergence; others might choose that path, particularly from a defensive standpoint, but we intend to continue serving both markets separately.

speaker: Bill C. Shope
title: Analyst, Goldman Sachs
content: Tim, there's been quite a bit of concern both in the press and within the investment community around carrier subsidies. And I think the concerns are generally twofold: First, that carriers will attempt to stretch out the replacement cycle. And second, that over time, carriers across the globe will attempt to reduce subsidies significantly. I mean, how do you think about this risk? And do you think there are factors that could pressure subsidies going forward? And how would that impact Apple?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Our focus is on creating the best smartphone in the world, one that offers an exceptional user experience that customers want to use every day. Ultimately, carriers, or most of them, want to provide what their customers desire, and that's their motivation. The key for Apple is to keep producing great products that people want, and we are fully committed to this, innovating at an impressive pace. From a carrier's standpoint, it's crucial to recognize that the subsidy isn't significant compared to the total monthly payments over a two-year contract. The difference in cost between the iPhone and other phones is even smaller. The iPhone also presents distinct advantages for carriers; for instance, many carrier executives have indicated that churn rates among iPhone customers are the lowest of all the phones they sell, which brings substantial financial benefits for the carrier. Our engineering teams work diligently to enhance data efficiency, making the iPhone far superior in this regard compared to other smartphones with extensive app ecosystems. Most importantly, the iPhone is the ideal device to encourage customers using traditional mobile phones to make the leap to smartphones. This represents a significant opportunity for Apple and our carrier partners, resulting in a great experience for customers. There are benefits all around, and many of these points are overlooked in discussions about subsidies.

speaker: Bill C. Shope
title: Analyst, Goldman Sachs
content: That's helpful. I had one other follow-up question, if I could. I appreciate the user stats you gave us on iCloud. But can you give us any color, now it's been out for a few months, on how consumers are actually using iCloud? And in particular, are you seeing a big uptake in iTunes Match and paid storage additions? And how should we think about that?

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Customers are fully utilizing all the features of iCloud, and the response has been outstanding. Feedback has been excellent. While there is a gradual increase in storage usage, it’s important to note that we only launched iCloud in October. Since then, we have welcomed over 125 million users to the service, and they are actively creating and storing documents, music, and other data. We anticipate that storage growth will increase over time. Our main objective was not to simply sell more storage; we believe Match is an excellent product that we encourage everyone to use, although it is a paid service. Our goal was to enhance customer satisfaction across the entire ecosystem and platform of our iOS devices and Macs, which is the reason for launching iCloud. We are thrilled that just a couple of months in, we have over 125 million users globally on iCloud.

speaker: Charles Eugene Munster
title: Analyst, Piper Jaffray
content: If you could dig a little bit more into what's going on in China. I know you gave some high-level numbers. But is this increased distribution points, is it just price elasticity of lower-priced 3GS? Is it more people in China having money? All of the above? Anything that you can tell us to explain this vertical growth?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Gene, it was an incredible quarter in China. The revenue reached a record $7.9 billion in Greater China, more than tripling year-over-year, bringing the first half revenue for Greater China to $12.4 billion. This contrasts with last year's full-year revenue of $13.3 billion. It's astonishing to see such success. One of the factors driving this is the pent-up demand for the iPhone 4S, especially since we launched in mainland China in January this year, which meant it did not contribute to Q1 numbers but added to Q2. Additionally, we are seeing strong demand for the iPad 2. While the new iPad has not yet shipped in mainland China, it is being shipped in Hong Kong. The impact of both products has significantly boosted Mac sales, which rose over 60% year-over-year, compared to a market growth rate of about 6%. Our point of sale presence has expanded, with Mac sales up 70% year-over-year, though we only have 1,800 outlets across Greater China, indicating substantial room for growth. iPhone sales increased to over 11,000 units, representing a 138% rise, but this figure is still much smaller than in the U.S., suggesting that China presents a larger opportunity in the coming years. The iPad is currently available in only 2,500 points of sale, so while we've made significant progress, we believe there is still much more potential.

speaker: Charles Eugene Munster
title: Analyst, Piper Jaffray
content: Was the iPhone mix in China different than the rest of the world? Or how was it different?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: I don't have that information readily available, but I recall that it was not significantly different. However, it's important to note that the iPhone 4S had just been launched during the quarter. Typically, when a new product is released within a quarter, you can expect the sales mix to lean more towards that new product.

speaker: Charles Eugene Munster
title: Analyst, Piper Jaffray
content: And just one final quick question on iTunes content. It seems that there's kind of this logjam to getting more TV shows and movies and the rentals, and it's been a little bit of a slow pace of improvement. How important is getting better content on iTunes? And what's going to break that logjam?

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Gene, it's Peter. We're actually thrilled with the rate that we're adding content into iTunes. This is something that we have to do country by country, so it takes a bit of time to put in place. We have the largest catalog of songs and movies available anywhere, over 28 million songs. And this led to almost $1.9 billion of revenue in the March quarter, which was up 35% year-over-year. So we're thrilled with the progress that we're making in iTunes and customers love it.

speaker: Benjamin A. Reitzes
title: Analyst, Barclays
content: Tim, another significant issue beyond the subsidy question you just addressed involves shortages. There are discussions about potential Qualcomm shortages in the next couple of quarters and possible constraints even at year-end for some valuable products that could benefit you in the future. I understand you don’t comment on upcoming products, but this is a significant concern. Can you provide some insight into whether you anticipate being able to secure more than your fair share of product in the long term? Additionally, do you foresee any major bottlenecks on the horizon in that area or with any components in the long run?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Tough question to answer, Ben. Obviously, we're aware of the lithography transition issue that you mentioned with 28 nanometer. We currently do not use 28-nanometer parts. But as you also know, we don't comment about future products, and so I can't talk about the future part. Generally, outside of this, we work very closely with our supplier partners and do everything that we can do to get supply. And sometimes, we're successful with that, and sometimes we're not. And so you can bet that we are focused on anything that we think may impact us and trying to push every button within our disposal to work on it.

speaker: Benjamin A. Reitzes
title: Analyst, Barclays
content: Okay. Well, I appreciate that. And then my follow-up is regarding Walmart. They were actually just in our building in a conference here talking about how they're moving from one store in Arkansas now to 25 stores. And they seem really pleased with the "store within a store" concept. How is it going? And when can you be in all 10,000 stores?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: There's no plan to be in 10,000. And so we're trying some things. And as you know, that doesn't include the Mac. And so we're trying some things and seeing how it goes. And they've been a very good partner for us on iPod and have been selling iPods for a while and are an increasingly more substantial partner in the iPad space as well and an evolving partner on iPhone. And so we're working with them and enjoy working with them and hope to continue expanding.

speaker: Keith F. Bachman
title: Analyst, BMO Capital Markets
content: Tim, could you provide more details about iPhones in the Asia Pacific region, particularly in China? Is the supply and demand there balanced? Additionally, with an increase in iPhone inventory of 2.6 million units, will that number decrease in the June quarter? Any comments you could share on that would be appreciated. I also have a follow-up question.

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Yes, let me address your last question. Regarding the 2.6 million, I want to clarify that our goal was to increase channel inventory throughout the quarter. As you may remember, we finished December with just 6 million units in the channel due to a significant backlog, particularly concerning the iPhone 4S. Our objective is to maintain inventory levels between 4 million and 6 million. The addition of the 2.6 million units helped us reach that target by the end of the quarter. We believe we ended the quarter with supply and demand in balance. Thanks to the excellent execution by our operations team, we successfully addressed most of the supply-demand issues in various countries by the end of January. We experienced an exceptional start to the quarter, significantly reducing the iPhone 4S backlog and also launching in China. Overall, it was a remarkable beginning for us this quarter.

speaker: Keith F. Bachman
title: Analyst, BMO Capital Markets
content: On China specifically. It sounds like China can still be a help. Or it sounds like China is still supply-demand imbalanced. But I wanted to see if you could add some thoughts there in terms of iPhones.

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: No. China is not supply-demand imbalanced on iPhone. On iPad, worldwide, we're supply constrained on the new iPad, both coming out of last quarter. And to give you a current view, we're still supply constrained on the new iPad. Demand has been incredibly robust, and we are selling them as fast as we can make them, as Peter mentioned earlier. In China, I believe on a macro basis, China has an enormous number of people moving into the higher income groups, middle class, if you will. And this is creating a demand for goods, not just Apple's but other companies' goods as well. And so I think there's a tremendous opportunity for companies that understand China, and we're doing everything we can to understand it and serve the market as good as we can.

speaker: Keith F. Bachman
title: Analyst, BMO Capital Markets
content: It certainly seems so. Tim, for my follow-up from Bill Shope's question, there have been some changes in Spain in particular on the behavior of their carriers and the economics. And Vodafone has actually changed some of their subsidy levels. It's only been about 30 days or 35 days, but have you seen any changes in demand levels in the Spanish market as a consequence of some of the activities of the carriers? And that's it for me.

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Yes. Keith, Spain has been challenging for us and likely for many companies as well. Our revenues did increase in Spain last quarter, but significantly less than our growth in Europe or globally. The issues in Spain stem from its difficult economic situation, which I view as a unique case. To clarify, there's some confusion regarding what has occurred. The carriers have maintained subsidies for their existing customers, but they have reduced subsidies for new customers. It's important to note that not all carriers in that market made this change; only a few did. Therefore, I wouldn’t necessarily consider this a reflection of the overall market.

speaker: Mark A Moskowitz
title: Analyst, JP Morgan
content: A question for Peter. Peter, can you provide a little more framework or context for us in terms of understanding how the segments dovetail with the 13% sequential revenue decline in the guidance? In terms of that bogey, what product segments could be higher in terms of decline or less than the decline?

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: We expect an increase in iPhone sales year-over-year but a decrease sequentially due to the reasons Tim and I mentioned. We built channel inventory in the March quarter and are balancing supply and demand as we exit March, following a strong January. For iPad, we anticipate a significant year-over-year and sequential sales increase. Additionally, I want to mention our gross margin guidance for the June quarter, which is set at 41.5%. We believe that about two-thirds of the sequential decline will be mainly due to a higher mix of iPads and Macs, benefiting from a full quarter of the current iPad lineup, along with leveraging the sequentially lower revenue. The remaining difference is expected to stem from factors that positively impacted the March quarter gross margin but are not anticipated to recur in June.

speaker: Nancy Paxton
title: Senior Director of Investor Relations
content: And Mark, did you have a second question?

speaker: Mark A Moskowitz
title: Analyst, JP Morgan
content: Yes. Tim, Tim, can you hear me?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Yes, I can now.

speaker: Mark A Moskowitz
title: Analyst, JP Morgan
content: Okay, great. Sorry about that. I wanted to discuss your recent flexibility in cash usage and your commentary during the earnings call. How should we view potential opportunities for increased flexibility regarding patent disputes? Is there a point where Apple might consider settling and focus on innovation instead of engaging in ongoing litigation? Are there possibilities for that?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: I've always disliked litigation, and that feeling hasn't changed. We want people to create their own innovations. If we could reach an agreement that ensures this and provides a fair resolution for past issues, I would much prefer to settle rather than engage in a dispute. However, it's crucial that Apple does not take on the role of being the developer for everyone. We need individuals to come up with their own ideas.

speaker: Shannon S. Cross
title: Analyst, Cross Research
content: My first question is just going back to iCloud. Perhaps Tim, if you can talk a little bit more about feedback from customers? Curious sort of average number of devices of customers that customers are putting up or maybe percent of users attaching more than one device. Just sort of what's the initial feedback? And then I have a follow-up.

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Shannon, it's Peter. I don't want to frustrate you, but, well, we have, of course, the data that you're asking for, but we don't want to help our competitors. And so it's not something that we're going to provide probably. The feedback that we're getting from customers on iCloud is just it's off the charts. They're loving it. And the fact that we could be here on the conference call with you in April just 5 or 6 months after introducing the service and have 125 million people around the world using it every day, I think, speaks for itself.

speaker: Shannon S. Cross
title: Analyst, Cross Research
content: My follow-up question is about R&D. It increased by 45%, now exceeding $800 million. I'm interested to know if part of this growth is due to the acquisitions you've made, and if you could share your thoughts on R&D and investment levels. The increase suggests positive developments for upcoming products.

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Well, we view this as a good thing. We are investing in engineering to continue to bring out the most innovative products in the world to delight customers. We are making investments in our hardware and software engineering teams. We're shipping the best products that Apple has ever shipped today. And we've got some fabulous new products in the pipeline. So I'm very confident in the return that we're going to see on these investments.

speaker: Shannon S. Cross
title: Analyst, Cross Research
content: You used to give sort of an idea of percentage to software, percentage of hardware. Is there anything you can give there?

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Shannon, I'm sorry. I don't have that in front of me.

speaker: Shaw Wu
title: Analyst, Sterne Agee
content: Just a quick clarification. I understand you disclosed China in terms of the 4S shipping along with 21 countries early in January. What about China Telecom specifically? When did that launch?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Shaw, it's Tim. We launched with China Telecom in March. And in early part of March, we were at a supply-demand balance with them prior to the end of the quarter. We're very happy to be working with them.

speaker: Scott D. Craig
title: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
content: Peter, on the OpEx side, that's an area where you guys have been getting a fair amount of leverage. If you look year-over-year, it's down pretty significantly as a percentage of sales. So I'm just curious on your thoughts going forward, maybe not just next quarter but sort of how do you think about the OpEx leverage longer term? And then, Tim, can you just kind of take us through the components like you do on most quarter calls and where you're seeing some pricing better than expected and maybe worse than expected and put that in the context of going forward as well?

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Yes, it's Peter. As I mentioned in response to Shannon's question, we are investing in research and development to bring the most innovative products to market. We are also allocating funds to marketing, advertising, opening more of our own retail locations, and expanding our indirect sales channels globally to boost sales. Additionally, we are investing in infrastructure to support our growth and in stock-based compensation for our employees. We are very confident in the investments we are making. We are focused on the long term and believe in the returns we will achieve from these investments.

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: In terms of component costs for the quarter we just finished, Q2 component costs were better than we had planned, which helped us exceed our gross margin guidance. Displays and NAND flash were the primary contributors to the favorable commodity cost benefit. Looking at the June quarter and what we factored into our guidance, NAND and mobile DRAM supply continued to exceed demand, which leads us to expect pricing will remain favorable. For most LCDs, we anticipate that pricing will stabilize as the market reaches a supply-demand balance. The hard drive market has also moved to a supply-demand balance, and while we expect market pricing to decline, it will still be higher than the pre-flood levels seen during the tragedy in Thailand. Most other components are expected to align with or exceed historical trends.

speaker: Kulbinder Garcha
title: Analyst, Credit Suisse
content: Just a clarification, Pete. Did you say that 2/3 of the sequential gross margin decline was basically due to products? And did I hear that right? Because it seems like quite a rapid drop, and I'm just wondering how much conservatism is in your gross margin guidance. And then I have a follow-up for Tim afterwards.

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Sure, Kulbinder, the 2/3 that I talked about, the sequential decline, we see as being driven by a higher mix of iPads and Macs, a full quarter of selling the current iPad or the current iPad lineup, and then a loss of leverage on the sequentially lower revenue. So those 3 factors we see driving 2/3 of the sequential decline.

speaker: Kulbinder Garcha
title: Analyst, Credit Suisse
content: Okay, great. And then, Tim, just a question on the enterprise side. You mentioned a couple of times how the iPad is being taken into new markets, new verticals, whether it's because of the price point of the innovation. I'm just wondering specifically what resources is Apple dedicating to have a much more direct relationship with the enterprise? Can you speak on what's changed in the last 6 or 12 months and what you think you need to do to become a more credible or significant enterprise player?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: Initially, we focused on collaborating with the Fortune 500 and the Global 500 to get the iPad certified for their specific enterprise needs. I'm happy to share that 94% of the Fortune 500 and 75% of the Global 500 are either testing or deploying iPads. These figures are remarkable for a product that's only been on the market for 24 months. We're now shifting our attention from initial certification to deepening our engagement with these accounts. Peter mentioned some of our recent successes in his opening comments. These achievements span multiple sectors, including government and education, as well as various functions within enterprises. It's the most widespread product adoption I've seen throughout my career in the enterprise sector. Consequently, we are allocating more resources in Field Engineering and sales teams to directly engage with these customers. Additionally, we collaborate with our carrier and reseller partners to provide both products and services to these clients.

speaker: Chris Whitmore
title: Analyst, Deutsche Bank
content: Hello? Can you hear me?

speaker: Nancy Paxton
title: Senior Director of Investor Relations
content: Yes, we can.

speaker: Chris Whitmore
title: Analyst, Deutsche Bank
content: Okay, sorry about that. If I take your revenue guidance and the comments you made around gross margin at face value, it seems to imply that you expect iPhone unit sales to be down about 10 million units quarter-on-quarter. First, is that in the right ballpark? And secondly, are you just being conservative with respect to the outlook? Or have you seen a change in the end demand environment for the phone?

speaker: Peter Oppenheimer
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Chris, let me sort of go in reverse order. We are incredibly confident in our business, our strategy and what we're doing. When we give you guidance, we give you guidance that we have reasonable confidence in achieving. And finally, we do expect a sequential decline in iPhone sales driven by the fact that we built 2.6 million units of channel inventory in the March quarter, which we needed to do. We're now within our target range of 4 to 6 weeks, and we entered the March quarter with significant backlog, as we talked about, in January. And we're able to fulfill that and launch 20 countries in the month of January. So –- we have immense confidence in what we're doing and are very pleased with the way our business is performing.

speaker: Chris Whitmore
title: Analyst, Deutsche Bank
content: A follow-up, if I could, on iPad. It is supply constrained across many geos, as you talked about. Is there a specific component issue? Do you have visibility on resolution? When do you expect to be able to meet demand in the iPad?

speaker: Timothy D. Cook
title: Chief Executive Officer
content: It's hard to answer meet the demand. What I'm confident about, however, is that we will be able to supply a significant number of iPads during the quarter, and I feel very, very confident about that. It's tough to know precisely that it will balance until you get there, but I'm very confident with the improving supply and that the total number will be very significant.

title: Senior Director of Investor Relations
content: Thank you, Chris. A replay of today's call will be available for 2 weeks as a Podcast on the iTunes Store, as a webcast on Apple.com/investor and via telephone. content: Ladies and gentlemen, that does conclude today's presentation. We do thank everyone for your participation.

title: Operator
content: Good day, everyone, and welcome to this Apple Incorporated Third Quarter Fiscal Year 2012 Earnings Release Call. Today’s call is being recorded. speaker: Nancy Paxton
title: Senior Director of Investor Relations
content: Thank you. Good afternoon, and thanks to everyone for joining us.
