So, we do actually and we keep the flexibility to make sure that we really feed the winner so that they keep the momentum as you've seen, for example in Android in the last 24 months, which has been tremendous. All right. Thank you for your question. Connie, we probably have time for two or three more – two more questions. So let's go for the second last.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Thank you. And we will take our last question from Mark May from Needham & Company.

speaker: Mark May
title: Analyst
content: Thanks. A big picture question about data, because that seems to be an increasing factor of differentiation in growth for online ad companies. How does Google think generally about leveraging user data, both to better target ads and how to stay competitive with those like Facebook and Microsoft and Yahoo! that are leveraging data possibly more so than like Google is today? And I think this is particularly relevant for using search data for your display business, but we would love to get your thoughts on that.

speaker: Eric Schmidt
title: CEO
content: We have a pretty strong opinion that we are not going to do very much of it. The reason is that we take our end user data privacy incredibly seriously, and the trust that people have with respect to giving us that information, both their search histories as well as other piece of information, they get very upset very, very quickly if we, in their view, misuse it. So what we typically tell people is we are not going to do the kind of things that you could do with this, like in particular, use it to generate sort of strange apps against your history and things like that without your explicit permission, and we probably in many cases won't do it forever.

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: Thank you, Mark. Let's go to our last question, Connie.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: And we will take our final question from Marianne Wolk from Susquehanna.

speaker: Marianne Wolk
title: Analyst
content: Thanks very much. It looks like you did a great job converting a lot of the advertising on the content network over to display. Can you talk about to what extent that's now video-based and is that helping monetization rate significantly? And do you expect that to be sort of a 100% display shortly? Thank you.

speaker: Nikesh Arora
title: President, Global Sales Operations and Business Development
content: I have been waiting for the entire earnings call, Patrick, to talk about display. I am glad that Patrick and Jonathan have allowed us to disclose the run rate of $2.5 billion. I think this puts us in one of the top three display networks in the world. And I also believe that the technology suite we offer is second to none. So in terms of the video versus the other display formats, it is – primarily a lot of this is still display in terms of banner ads and other formats, and video is beginning to come into it. But we believe in the future there is going to be a lot more rich media involved into display network, because as we go forward you are going to see more and more monetization of video, whether it's on YouTube or other partner sites that's going to happen. So we believe the display network we offer has maximum frequency and maximum reach. We can reach people more times a day than anyone else. So, really excited about display. So, I was not sure what you meant by what becomes 100% of display?

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: Chief Financial Officer
content: And on the previous question – on the follow-up question, it was about – it's just the trailing quarter. So with that, thank you for your question, Marianne. Let me give you a couple of thoughts. One is, just want to reiterate that what we did today was give you a few indications of why we believe we are successful in these emerging businesses. These data points are not about giving you more information on the coming quarters, but more to give you the confidence about where we are investing and it's really fueling great growth rates and building meaningful businesses. I want to thank you Eric for taking the time. I know he is running for the plane, but it's terrific to have you on the call and take a few minutes with our analysts and shareholders. And then I also want to take a moment to thank all the Googlers for their hard work. I mean, all this strong performance is really on the back of fantastic work from our team worldwide, our great engineers, our great sales force, and our great support staff everywhere. So I just wanted to take from the OC, 40 just the time to thank them again on – in the public domain, because they do such a terrific job. With that, Connie, I'll let you close the call.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Thank you. And this concludes today's conference. We thank you for your participation.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Good day and welcome, everyone, to the Google Inc. Fourth Quarter 2010 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, I would like to turn the conference over to Jane Penner, Senior IR Manager. Please go ahead.

speaker: Jane Penner
title: Senior IR Manager
content: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to today's Fourth Quarter and Fiscal Year 2010 Earnings Conference Call. With us are Eric Schmidt, Chief Executive Officer and Chairman of the Board; Larry Page, Co-Founder and President, Products; Sergey Brin, Co-Founder and President, Technology; Patrick Pichette, Chief Financial Officer; Jonathan Rosenberg, Senior Vice President, Product Management; and Nikesh Arora, Senior Vice President and Chief Business Officer. This call is also being webcast from investor.google.com. A replay of the call will be available on our website in a few hours. Now let me quickly cover the Safe Harbor. Some of the statements we make today may be considered forward-looking including statements regarding our expected level of capital expenditures, Google's future and investments in our long-term growth and innovation and the expected performance of our business. These statements involve a number of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please note that these forward-looking statements reflect our opinions only as of the date of this presentation, and we undertake no obligation to revise or publicly release the results of any revision to these forward-looking statements in light of new information or future events. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed description of the risk factors that may affect our results. Please note that certain financial measures we use on this call, such as operating income and operating margin, are also expressed on a non-GAAP basis and have been adjusted to exclude charges related to stock-based compensation. We have also adjusted our net cash provided by operating activities to remove capital expenditures, which we refer to as free cash flow. Our GAAP results and reconciliations of non-GAAP to GAAP measures can be found in our earnings press release. With that, I will now turn the call over to Eric.

speaker: Eric Schmidt
title: CEO
content: Thank you very much, Jane, and thanks, everybody, for getting on our call. Your time is very valuable. I'm really glad that you all could join us for our quarterly call as reasonably scheduled. We've jumped on the call to talk about the other announcement of this afternoon, which I think everybody is getting a chance to read. We've had a very strong quarter and a very strong year. And I think as our results show today, our outlook is very, very bright. Larry and Sergey and I spent a lot of time talking about how to run everything. The last decade has of course been fantastic, and we anticipate this will continue. How can we run the company even better? After a long series of conversations, we decided to make some changes in the way we are structuring, the way we actually operate things. Historically, we've always been running the decisions together, and ultimately, it adds delay in the way we make decisions. It's actually better to clarify it. So the proposal, which the board has completely approved, is by elevating me and by having Larry run things day-to-day, with Sergey focusing on the areas he's going to talk about. We think that this will produce even better success for the corporation. And of course, we're going to do all this by April. So, Larry, do you want to introduce a little bit about your thoughts?

speaker: Larry Page
title: Co-Founder and President, Products
content: Well, first, I want to really congratulate Eric. He's done an outstanding job leading Google for the last decade. I don't think when Sergey and I started the company, we could have possibly imagined we would have a better leader for the company. We all owe a great debt to Eric. I think the results really speak for themselves. There is no debate about that at all. There’s really no one else in the universe that could have accomplished what Eric has done. Eric is really a tremendous leader, and I've learned a lot from him over the years. I think his advice and efforts going forward as Executive Chairman will be invaluable to me and to the company as I start this new role. Google is an incredible opportunity. When we started Google, people thought we were coming in too late, with a lot of other search engines already existing. The Internet and people's computing life are still at the very early stages. I could not be more excited about moving us forward, and we're really only at the beginning. I can't wait to get it started.

speaker: Eric Schmidt
title: CEO
content: Thank you, Larry. Sergey, do you want to talk a little bit about what you would like to get done in this new structure?

speaker: Sergey Brin
title: Co-Founder and President, Technology
content: I'd like to first mention that I had a great time working together with Larry for about 15 years and with Eric for about a decade. Both of them have really inspired me and moved me, and I'm looking forward to many more decades of work together. Now, as we have tried to clarify our respective roles now, I would like to work more on my personal passions, which correspond to several significant new products that I hope to tell you about in the future. I'm not going to repeat the accusations of being vaporware just recently in the press, so I don't want to repeat that error. I hope to tell you about them in the future when I'm ready to show you something. But nonetheless, it's really a privilege to work with these two gentlemen, to continue to work with them at this company that I've been really proud to be part of all this time.

speaker: Eric Schmidt
title: CEO
content: Thank you very much. And as for myself, I want to have a chance to work on the things that I'm most interested in, taking a more strategic view of things. I'm going to focus on customers, partners, various government communications, and external issues more than the internal issues that I've historically been focusing on. So that's a significant improvement in the kind of things that I can do with my time. I want to say very clearly that I believe Larry is ready. He has been working in this area for a long time. His ideas are very interesting and clever, and it's time for him to have a shot at running things and doing it. I'm sure he'll do a fantastic job. A decade goes by very fast when you work in such a wonderful partnership as this has been, and I'm quite sure that this partnership will continue. We’re friends, we’re co-workers, and we have a common vision. I don't anticipate any material change in any of our strategies or anything. We tend to agree on pretty much everything. But I do believe that as a result of this, we'll operate and execute the business even better. So with that, I thought maybe we should have a few questions before we rush off, and then, Patrick, thank you so much for accommodating us on to your call.

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: It's our pleasure. Jay, if you don't mind, we'll have two sets of questions for this afternoon. We'll take a few questions now because we have Larry, Sergey, and Eric. After that, we'll close that section of the call, let them return to work, and then we'll take the regular call as we usually proceed. So, Jay, if I can ask you to give us the instructions to take a couple of questions for Eric, Larry, and Sergey?

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: We'll go first to James Mitchell from Goldman Sachs.

speaker: James Mitchell
title: Analyst
content: I guess one question I have just stemming from the results from the movements perhaps, when I look at the investments in 1118 Avenue in New York City, do you feel that Google is now at a point where in order to continue facilitating the growth of the Internet, that there will be a land grab for desirable physical locations?

speaker: Larry Page
title: Co-Founder and President, Products
content: I think our primary reason for purchasing the building there was not the Internet infrastructure but rather the office space that we really enjoy using. The Internet tenants are great, well-paying tenants. We appreciate having them there, but that's not the primary reason why we purchased the building.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our next question comes from Spencer Wang with Credit Suisse.

speaker: Spencer Wang
title: Analyst
content: Just a big picture question for Eric. You mentioned that one of your areas of focus will be on government outreach, and it seems like Google may have come under a little more regulatory scrutiny over the past several years. So I was wondering if you could talk a little bit about your strategy with regulators to ensure that Google can continue to expand as necessary?

speaker: Eric Schmidt
title: CEO
content: The simple answer is that we're talking to them. A lot of the problems we've been having are that people don't actually understand what we really do and what we don't do, and some of our competitors are assisting in that misinformation. So part of our core strategy is literally to communicate. This is what we're doing. We're trying to be as transparent and collaborative as possible. I will tell you very clearly that the regulators have a proper job to do. They’re there for a reason and we respect that. So far, we've been quite successful by just taking the time to help people understand. We're sensitive to the close lines. This is where we get too close to something and we try to stay away from that. We stay well within the safety zone of our operations, with respect to legal issues and competitive issues. We also argue very strongly that the things we're doing are very pro-competitive. I genuinely believe that, and I’ll be telling people a lot of that for a long time as expected.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our next question will come from Imran Khan with JPMorgan.

speaker: Imran Khan
title: Analyst
content: Larry, as you become the CEO, I think it was just a very interesting juncture of Google's life cycle. There are many questions from investors regarding the proliferation of social networking and how the traffic source to these platforms is becoming more prevalent. As Google gets to the next level, how do you think about real-time search in relation to social networking platforms? How do you think Google will become the point of play where users can send traffic to other places?

speaker: Eric Schmidt
title: CEO
content: Sergey, you've been driving most of this, and maybe, Larry, you could comment as well.

speaker: Sergey Brin
title: Co-Founder and President, Technology
content: Yes. I think that you pointed out two important trends. One is the notion of real-time, and the other is the broad notion of social in terms of identity, relationships, and so forth. Both of those are very important to search. In fact, you've seen us roll out functionality along those lines over the past year. First, we now have the real-time updates built into our Search, including Twitter and other sources. You've also seen us deploy social search, which allows you to find search results related to people you know and friends of their friends. You see those right in the main Search Results on the Web. But I think this is really just the tip of the iceberg, and I think there is far more opportunity. We've touched just 1% of the capabilities that could be deployed in that realm. You should expect us to continue to develop those kinds of capabilities.

speaker: Eric Schmidt
title: CEO
content: Larry, did you want to add anything to that?

speaker: Larry Page
title: Co-Founder and President, Products
content: I mean, the last part of what Sergey said really resonates with me. If you think about the next five years of what your life will be like online and socially, and what things the tools will be able to do, we're only at the very, very early stages of that. I'm incredibly excited about the possibilities to come.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our next question comes from Justin Post of Bank of America.

speaker: Justin Post
title: Analyst
content: We've noticed a lot of changes on the site, moving you farther down the purchasing funnel. We've heard some regulatory pushbacks, so maybe this is a question for you, Eric, but also there are potential advertiser complaints. I'm just wondering how the changes in your Search Ad results are driving your revenues and helping to drive the strong growth? How are you dealing with the advertisers and the regulatory environment on some of those changes that might be replacing some of the functionality of other websites?

speaker: Eric Schmidt
title: CEO
content: There's no question that our extraordinary results are partly coming from algorithmic improvements that we implement continuously. Our basic strategy, of course, is to have the right ad in the right spot done exactly right every time. We do literally billions of these every day. That’s the great magic of Google. We've looked very carefully at how we make decisions about which ads go where. We're pretty happy with the choices we make in terms of ranking ads. There have been some competitor complaints, and we are conducting thorough reviews. But so far, we’re quite happy with the choices, and we believe they will pass the necessary complaints that people are raising. So with that, I think we’ve run over time. I appreciate everybody letting us come in and do this. I wanted to say that it’s been a great privilege to be the CEO for 10 years, literally a decade. A decade is a long time to be a CEO. I’m looking forward to this new role, a more strategic role where I can work on new things, which I’m excited about. I'm looking forward to working with my, literally, best friends and partners, Larry and Sergey. I hope you understand how powerful this triumvirate has been to us, and how much it means to us as individuals.

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: Absolutely. Thank you so much, Larry, Sergey, Eric, for taking the time to join us this afternoon. We will now mute your lines and jump right into our more regular conversations. I will start with my opening remarks and the financials. Jonathan will give us his read of the year, and then we'll be joined by Nikesh for our Q&A section. So how else to talk about 2010 in Q4 as a phenomenal ending to a very good year at Google? Our incredibly strong performance in Q4 and 2010 overall is a testimonial to the fundamental trends in the digital economy. These trends are fueling huge opportunities for innovation and growth at Google but also in the entire ecosystem. One of these profound trends is the shift from offline to online advertising, which continues at a quite rapid clip. You've seen this fueling growth in our core Search business and across the board as well. A case in point is revenue growth in our core accelerated strongly in the second half of 2010, which is particularly impressive given that Q4 2009 was itself a very strong quarter. In addition, investments in our newer businesses, the usual suspects of Display, Mobile, and Enterprise, are also creating a second powerful growth engine for Google. Jonathan will provide more details on that shortly. But at a high level, I just want to make it clear how can we not be happy with the overall performance and trajectories of 2010, and that basis be excited about our prospects for 2011 and beyond. So let me now turn for specifics about the quarter's performance.

speaker: Jonathan Rosenberg
title: Senior Vice President, Product Management
content: Thanks, Patrick. We've certainly had a great year at Google, and I think some of it stems from the unique way we manage our product and engineering machine. When we hire product managers, they often ask, 'So how do we measure success at Google?' I always tell them it’s simple. At the end of the year, we make a list of all your successes and failures. You're then measured on the sum of your successes and how much you learn from your failures. At the beginning of 2010, one of our concerns was that as we scaled, this approach might lead us to be spread too thin. We had to put more focus behind fewer arrows. So we made some changes that I think addressed this concern without affecting the basic philosophy of how we've always managed product and engineering at Google. Let’s talk about what we changed. At the beginning of the year, we decided to double down on the core; that’s Search and Search Ads. I think the financial numbers you’re seeing reflect the success of that bet. Behind those numbers is a relentless stream of new features and product innovations. For example, we made a big effort this year to make Search more interactive, and you can see that with Google Instant. More recently, we've made previews instant as well. Earlier in the year, we launched new user interfaces for Web Search and Image Search to make it easier and more intuitive to work with results after you run a search. We’re also making Search more intelligent. We've made several changes to results so now you can see things like concert schedules or answers to questions highlighted right in the snippets. We’re also rolling out Place Search so when we know you're looking for something in the neighborhood, we’ll pull reviews, webpages, addresses, and photos together for you. We also doubled down on the Ad side. This past year, we launched several new ad formats, including Sitelinks, seller rating ads, and more recently, product listings with photos and prices. It makes sense that if I'm shopping for something like a coffee maker, it’s helpful to see more information in the ad. The biggest boost of all came from good old-fashioned ad quality improvements. Q4 was our best quarter in years from a quality standpoint; we launched over 20 updates which led to gains that were nearly double those we’d normally see in a strong quarter.

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: So, in summary, we are incredibly pleased with our performance in 2010 and optimistic about our trajectory for '11 and beyond. Accordingly, we will continue to invest aggressively in a bold innovation agenda. So with that, I will turn it over to Jonathan to speak about the product muscles in Q4 in 2010. Jonathan, all yours?

speaker: Jonathan Rosenberg
title: Senior Vice President, Product Management
content: Thanks, Patrick. To quickly summarize, we expect more of the same in 2011. We will double down again on the core of Search and Search Ads, feed the 2010 winners—Display, YouTube, Enterprise, and Android—with even greater financial rigor and cross-functional coordination across the world. But I'm excited about the prospects of our newest businesses, Local and Commerce. In Local, over 5 million businesses have claimed their Google Place pages. We recently started testing a new ad product called Boost, which gives businesses a fast way to promote themselves online and connect with people searching for them. In Commerce, we're investing a lot to close the loop from online to offline shopping. I think as smartphones become ubiquitous and local businesses put their inventories online, I think this is the year where phones will play a big role in commerce. We will invest in hiring even more product managers and engineers, give them greater autonomy, and push them to work faster. Throughout the year we will tally our successes. I'll surely remind us of any failures so that we can keep learning from them. I hope you understand our sense of optimism from a product perspective for 2011.

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: Thank you, Jonathan. We will now turn it to Jay, and we will go to the Q&A section of this call. Jay, please give us the instructions?

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: And we'll go to Ben Schachter with Macquarie.

speaker: Benjamin Schachter
title: Analyst
content: Jonathan, I wanted to ask a question about Mobile, specifically how Google thinks about the differences between tablet users and smartphone users, and how those differences influence your high-level view of the overall evolving mobile market. And then Patrick, if you could address the sales and marketing line, which I think was somewhat unexpectedly high.

speaker: Jonathan Rosenberg
title: Senior Vice President, Product Management
content: Sure, Ben, we can take that in order. It’s probably easier to talk about initially how tablets and smartphones are similar. Both are growing at a terrific pace. The search usage on tablets tends to peak on weekends and dip on weekdays, so it's generally complementary to desktop usage. That suggests that people may use them more for personal purposes rather than business. Tablet users tend to search more for things like news and engage in more shopping-related topics compared to smartphone users. I think there’s some anecdotal data that they may convert better, but I haven't gone through all of that in detail. Tablets behave a little more like desktop devices since it’s easier to input information like a credit card. The major difference also is that the UI approaches are different, right? Apps designed for tablets are more tailored for the bigger screen. Both are taking off, and the revenue from tablets and smartphones reflects that.

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: I'll take the second question. If there's proof that we don’t just streamline our expense lines, but we act opportunistically and smartly, the marketing is a great example. Over the last 12 months, we've clearly shown how much the digital economy is in high gear. When that opportunity arrives, we need to jump on it and fuel it. For marketing, we have big platforms like Chrome and Chrome OS that can be incredibly successful if promoted, so why wouldn't we do it now? I hear from the financial community the other side, asking what we're doing with our money—well, we have great opportunities, so we’re jumping on it while the market is hot. Nikesh, could you provide some color commentary?

speaker: Nikesh Arora
title: Senior Vice President and Chief Business Officer
content: Thank you, Patrick. It’s important to understand we decided to put our foot on the pedal later this year. We focused on our small to medium-sized advertisers since that’s where much of our growth engine is going to come from in the future. A lot of the sales costs there are advertiser acquisition costs because once you bring them into our system, they stay for a while and continue generating more revenues. Some of the revenue performance you're seeing has been across small mid-tier channels, and that investment is beginning to bear fruit.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our next question comes from Mark Mahaney with Citi.

speaker: Mark Mahaney
title: Analyst
content: If I can ask a question about the local advertising play, you've been working on a couple of products and may have attempted an acquisition. Can you quantify this opportunity? Is this something that has always been part of the build-up plan? Did you see something in the last 12 months that indicates it’s time to accelerate efforts against local advertising? Also, do you feel you have all the assets in place, or are you still looking for more?

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: Let me just say, we do not talk about M&A. Local has always been part of our strategy. Nikesh can discuss our initiatives regarding products like Boost, or Jonathan can elaborate on them. Local is not a side event for us; it’s significant. One in every five searches has some local tendency. Now Jonathan?

speaker: Jonathan Rosenberg
title: Senior Vice President, Product Management
content: Sure, Mark. We’ve been very focused on Local since we acquired Keyhole, the original company behind Google Earth. The idea was to make the web a virtual mirror of the world at all times, which is much more useful when organized around places in the physical world. Recently, technology has made it possible through GPS and smartphones for us to understand where you are. We recognized more recently because smartphones are deployed more aggressively. We can provide you with relevant information about the places that you're near, which makes for appropriate contextual-oriented search.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our next question comes from Doug Anmuth with Barclays Capital.

speaker: Douglas Anmuth
title: Analyst
content: Patrick, can you talk a little more about your philosophy regarding the New York headquarters? I think this is the first time you've confirmed the purchase. Why do you need to own the headquarters rather than access it in another way? Why is this a good use of capital? Secondly, can you discuss building out more of a local salesforce in addition to the local products?

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: I’ll answer the first, Nikesh can talk about initiatives on the Local side. Look, we have 2,000 employees on site today in New York. Our business and engineering center is a large engineering center. If you think of it as an eastern hub with that many growing employees, it’s difficult to find a place that accommodates our needs and fits Google's culture. We don’t believe living in a tower where there’s a very small floor footprint is great for Google culture. Very few buildings in New York accommodate our needs. Replacing that building or moving would likely become prohibitively expensive. Finally, it gives us control over growing into that space, making it a wise investment. Nikesh, can you describe the Local strategy?

speaker: Nikesh Arora
title: Senior Vice President and Chief Business Officer
content: Regarding Local, there are three interpretations. First, we’ve always had local features to our ad products, allowing localization toward ads. Secondly, the way local often denotes smaller advertisers. We’ve created simplified products around Tags and Boost, making it easier for those advertisers to participate in the online economy. Third, we’ve partnered with companies selling advertising on our behalf to smaller advertisers. We will continue using all these efforts to pursue our Local strategy going forward.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our next question comes from Brian Pitz with UBS.

speaker: Brian Pitz
title: Analyst
content: Patrick, could you provide a rough organic revenue growth rate excluding acquisitions? Also, regarding Ads, are you seeing competitive share shifts in dollars from Search or Display towards other social platforms or applications?

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: I don’t have the breakdown and we don’t provide that detail. But I can tell you that all our core properties are growing well, including our new growth businesses. The numbers for google.com show 28% year-over-year growth; how can we not be happy with that kind of performance? Overall, we’re pleased with our revenue growth rate. Nikesh, please address the second piece.

speaker: Nikesh Arora
title: Senior Vice President and Chief Business Officer
content: It’s important to understand that Search has long been performance advertising, and so has a large chunk of Display. Newer players are often focused on brand display. The stronger trend is a shift of brand dollars from the offline sphere into the online world. There’s been less of an allocation shift within online, as all these methods are measurable, leading to better ROI for performance advertising, displayed and searched. So we see this trend continuing.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our next question comes from Ross Sandler with RBC Capital Markets.

speaker: Ross Sandler
title: Analyst
content: Patrick, regarding the Display business, financial statements of any publicly traded ad network show that these businesses typically peak out in operating margins around 20% to 25%. Do you think there's anything structurally different about Google’s approach in Display that could allow for higher operating margins? Or is this just the peak for that model?

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: On Display, the fundamental issue lies in whether you're on your network or optimizing for others' networks. If you consider YouTube, it's our own property, which usually results in different economics. You need to avoid comparing apples to oranges. While one type obviously has higher margins than the other, the question is about mix. Additionally, we have robust service offerings stemming from acquisitions like Teracent, which affect the financial picture.

speaker: Nikesh Arora
title: Senior Vice President and Chief Business Officer
content: Alongside that, the contribution of the Ad Exchange, bringing buyers and sellers together, allows for a serious uplift in revenue for participants. So while traditional Display has its structure, we see potential for improvement driven by the Ad Exchange.

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: Regarding the geographic performance, it’s a fantastic story. Acceleration this quarter comes from Germany, which has maintained its strength due to its economic developments that differ from the rest of Europe. I’m particularly excited about the turnaround we've achieved in Japan, where we’ve made significant efforts to bring in more partners and advertisers. The U.K. remains weak, but it remains a big market for us. Let’s also note that if we normalize our rest of world data for constant FX, the growth rate for that segment is over 30%, evidencing very positive momentum.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our next question comes from Scott Devitt with Morgan Stanley.

speaker: Scott Devitt
title: Analyst
content: Paid click growth on a percentage basis was the highest in two years. While you've mentioned better ads, targeting, and local monetization are factors—how much have Google Instant and smartphone/tablet queries contributed?

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: For paid click growth, look at a couple of factors. First, let me debunk the myth that Google Instant drives revenue growth; in fact, it’s neutral. Our growth comes from the economic recovery encouraging online spending. You can see that dramatically increased participation in auctions because more users are online. Platforms matter too, and features like mobile devices and Geo-targeting are also driving growth. Ultimately, our great ads, tuning, and monetization improvements also play critical roles.

speaker: Jonathan Rosenberg
title: Senior Vice President, Product Management
content: Aside from the ads quality improvements, we have new ad formats that boost click-through rates. I mentioned product listings, offer ads, and seller ratings; all have a significant impact. Most significantly, we had to pivot to a featured called Visible URL, moving the URL down to give it better visibility. We launched that figuring out people tend to skip and ignore ads when they see mixed character sets. Due to changes in Japan, we quickly expanded that feature globally. Our click-through rates went significantly up after its launch.

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: Certainly, this highlights just how much innovation remains in our ad formats and how much we can continue to improve our advertising practices.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our last question comes from Jeetil Patel with Deutsche Bank.

speaker: Jeetil Patel
title: Analyst
content: When looking at your customer revenue line from various segments, like Fortune 500 or Ad Age 100 versus Internet pureplays, I understand SMB was weak during the recession and are recovering. How are you viewing that segment today? Will there be a different approach or model for that segment going forward?

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: I'll let Nikesh handle that. Just one point—while you mentioned that SMBs were going down during the recession, they were actually moving upward. Nikesh, can you answer?

speaker: Nikesh Arora
title: Senior Vice President and Chief Business Officer
content: We're seeing strength from large advertisers, particularly as they strengthen their e-commerce offerings. For SMBs and mid-market advertisers, we've put a higher touch strategy for mid-tier customers because they've grown. For smaller advertisers, we’re working closely with Jonathan's team to enhance systematic improvements that help retain them while we work on reducing churn.

speaker: Jeetil Patel
title: Analyst
content: Do you think the business model or pricing would need to be different for the SMB segment? Possible percentage of sale or another method?

speaker: Nikesh Arora
title: Senior Vice President and Chief Business Officer
content: No, we're creating simpler products for them with different pricing. We want them to continue participating in the online economy without having to delve into complicated processes.

speaker: Operator
title: Operator
content: Our next question comes from Jason Maynard with Wells Fargo Securities.

speaker: Jason Maynard
title: Analyst
content: Regarding the Mobile business, we noted momentum last quarter. From a pricing perspective, what are you seeing from advertisers? And how about developments with NFC applications?

speaker: Patrick Pichette
title: CFO
content: Mobile search grew fourfold in the past year. It's evident that this market is cranking. There’s additional work ongoing, and Jonathan can expand on that.

speaker: Jonathan Rosenberg
title: Senior Vice President, Product Management
content: Click-to-Call ads are generating millions of calls. Advertisers such as DirectTV are successfully running campaigns focused around those. speaker: Operator
title: Operator

Strong performance everywhere gives us optimism regarding the digital economy. My coworkers, Jonathan and Nikesh, do an amazing job every day. Though it appears simple when discussing our results, they put in extraordinary efforts worldwide. Thanks for everything in 2010, and we're ready for a fantastic 2011.

speaker: Jonathan Rosenberg

speaker: Jane Penner

content: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to today's first quarter 2012 earnings conference call.
